Fourth Down: The Class You Quit
The quarterback just dropped the easy class. His ex-TA wants to fix him. He'd rather learn.
A senior quarterback quits the class that keeps athletes eligible. The grad TA who could've carried him has to learn to ask first.

Brody Hale has one semester left and a degree he could pass by smiling, so he drops the easy class and walks into Venture Lab knowing nothing. Ezra Kim, the grad TA who quietly asked off Brody's grading months ago, joins his team hungry for a seed grant and immediately starts moving his chair. This is not a story about a dumb jock rescued by a genius; it's two smart guys learning to split the work. You decide whether they build it together, side by side, or apart.
A fellow senior on the Venture Lab team—close enough to see the chair get moved, adult enough to say something.
Brody graduates with a degree he smiled through, and Ezra builds a company alone to prove he never needed anybody.

The Drop Form
Drop the easy class—and say what help you actually need
Lecture Hall B, after section
Tuesday, 4:50 PM
Section ends. Chairs scrape. Brody waits until the room empties, then sets a yellow drop form on the TA desk like it might go off.
I read the course number twice. Then I look at him over my glasses.
This is the class everyone takes to stay eligible.
I don't want a degree I can only pass by smiling.
That's annoyingly respectable.
I'm switching into Venture Lab. I'm behind on everything. Spreadsheets look at me, I look back, and nobody wins.
Dr. Patel grades you, not me—hasn't been me since fall. But I could write your first proposal. You pitch it. Everyone wins.
Everyone wins. That's exactly what the smiling was.
What does Brody tell him?
Admit you need a tutor. Ask him.
I don't need a writer. I need someone to explain it until I stop nodding like I get it.
I sign the form and slide it back. Then I write WED 8 PM on a sticky note and press it onto his thumb.
Bring questions. Dumb ones are cheaper.
Brody dropped the class and asked Ezra to tutor him in Venture Lab basics, with no ghostwriting.
Accept help—open lab hours only, for now.
Help, yes. But during open lab hours, with other people around. I want to not-know things where everybody can see.
Public humiliation as pedagogy. Bold. I'm there Thursdays.
He signs without arguing, which for Ezra Kim is practically a hug.
Brody accepted Ezra's help only during the lab's public open hours.
Turn down the ghostwriting. Go it alone.
No. If you write it, I just learned to smile at a different professor.
I sign harder than necessary. The pen tears the carbon copy.
Fine. When you're drowning, I'm in Room 214. I don't throw ropes. I throw office hours.
Brody refused Ezra's offer to write his proposal and started Venture Lab on his own.
Don't Move My Chair
Stop Ezra from deciding things for you
Venture Lab, the team table by the window
Thursday, 7:15 PM
Ezra has joined the team, because the seed grant needs a grad mentor and Ezra needs the seed grant. He has also been busy.
The deck's cover is a photo of Brody in pads. Brody's chair has been moved to the front, facing where the judges will sit.
I restructured. You're the story, I'm the numbers. Judges love a brave quarterback who quit the easy class. Just say it the way I wrote it.
I look at the chair. Then the photo. Then the script, which has my feelings in bullet points.
You don't get to call me brave and then move my chair.
I was helping.
Ask first.
The rest of the lab goes very quiet, the way people do when they're pretending to type.
How does Brody handle it?
Move the chair back. Rebuild the plan together.
I drag my chair back to the table, next to his, and flip the script facedown.
Ask me what I want to pitch. Then I'll ask you what the numbers say.
I ask. It takes forty minutes. At the door I turn back, which I never do.
Asking again: library, study room nine, Thursday after close. Bring your worst draft. I'll bring mine. Nobody gets to be the smart one.
Brody and Ezra rebuilt the pitch plan together; Ezra asked him to trade worst drafts in the library Thursday.
Keep his structure. Write your own words.
Keep the slide order. It's good. But the words about me come from me, or they don't go in.
Fine. And if your words are bad, I'm allowed to say so?
You're allowed to ask if you can say so.
…Noted. Library, Thursday, room nine. I'll show you my half. Fair warning: it's worse than I've been acting.
Brody kept Ezra's slide order but insisted on writing his own words; Ezra agreed to ask before editing him.
Refuse to be the cover photo.
I leave the front chair empty and take the back row with my laptop.
I'm not your mascot. Pitch it with me as a teammate, or pitch it without me.
I delete the photo. My jaw does the thing. At 12:40 AM, I text him anyway.
Library, room nine, Thursday. Not to fix you. I think I broke the budget, and you're the only one who'd tell me.
Brody refused to be the face of the pitch; Ezra cut the photo and later asked Brody to look at his broken budget.
Two Bad Drafts
Own your half of the revision
Main library, study room nine
Thursday, 11:40 PM
Study room nine smells like dry-erase marker and somebody's abandoned burrito. Two drafts lie facedown on the table like bad poker hands.
I flip mine first. “Athletes need career help after sports.” Source: me. Sample size: me and my roommate.
I flip mine. Eighteen months of costs, color-coded. Payroll, software, insurance. I forgot rent. I forgot we'd need to exist somewhere.
You forgot rent. You. The guy who color-codes his pens.
I thought being the smart one meant never needing you.
Congratulations. You're terrible at that.
I laugh—an ugly, surprised honk—and my shoulders come down for the first time all semester.
He needs me. It should not feel this good to be needed for rent.
How do they fix the drafts?
Revise together. Sign your own sections.
I get real interviews. You get a real lease quote. Our names go on our own pages.
I split the whiteboard down the middle. BRODY on one side, EZRA on the other, one arrow between them labeled “argue here.”
They leave at 2 AM with a plan and the burrito, which nobody claims.
They agreed to revise together, each signing his own section: Brody on interviews, Ezra on costs.
Finish your halves apart. Swap notes Sunday.
I think I need to do mine without you in the room. Not because of you. Because of me.
Understood. Sunday, notes only. I'll write them in pencil, like a coward.
They split the table down the middle and work in companionable silence until the lights blink their closing warning.
They chose to finish their sections separately and trade notes on Sunday.
Fix his budget yourself. Don't ask.
While he's in the hall on a call, I open his sheet, Google average rent, and add a line. I feel incredibly smart.
I come back and see it. I don't say anything for a full minute.
That's the wrong number. It's also exactly what I did to you. …Huh.
Brody added a rent line to Ezra's budget without asking; Ezra caught it, and both recognized the pattern.
Submit a Pilot
Shrink the project to what's actually true—and split the work in writing
Venture Lab, next to the jammed printer
Monday, 8:20 AM—grant deadline at noon
The grant application sits between two coffees. Box 4 says 200 clients in Year One. It has been saying that for a week.
We can't promise this many clients.
I wanted it to look ready.
It's not.
Down the hall, the printer jams, as if in solidarity.
Then we submit a pilot. Twenty athletes, one semester, real outcomes.
I'll do the interviews. All twenty. In person.
I'll fix the cost sheet. With rent. Rent is now my entire personality.
What does Brody put on paper?
Sign the pilot. Write down who does what.
I print it in box 7 in block capitals: INTERVIEWS—B. HALE. COSTS—E. KIM.
I initial beside it. It's the least impressive thing I've ever submitted. I've never been prouder of a document.
They submitted an honest twenty-athlete pilot with the division of work written into the application.
Ask for an extension. Get it right.
Let's email the lab for forty-eight hours. I'd rather be late than fake.
Extensions are for people who— …Fine. Asking first: can I write the email?
Yeah. You write a great email. It's kind of your whole thing.
They requested a forty-eight-hour extension to rebuild the application as a pilot; Ezra asked before writing the email.
Pull out of the grant. Build it anyway.
We don't need their money to find out if this works. I can start interviews Friday.
I stare at the form. Twenty thousand dollars. Also a number I made up.
Okay. No grant. But I'm coming to the interviews. Someone has to take notes you can read.
They withdrew from the grant cycle and began the pilot interviews unfunded.
When the Jersey Comes Off
Say out loud who built what
Business school atrium, Showcase Night
Friday, 6:30 PM, three weeks later
Folding chairs, a banner, and Coach Dwyer in the second row. He didn't RSVP. He came anyway.
Before they go up, Coach catches Brody's elbow: “Tell 'em the Iowa drive. People love the Iowa drive.”
I click past the photo of me in pads. The next slide is twenty faces—what they studied, where they landed, what they wish someone had told them.
I want something left when the jersey comes off. So did every guy on this slide.
A judge asks the money question. Ezra stands before Brody can answer.
The financial model was a disaster until Brody's interviews told us what athletes actually pay for. We revised it together. The good parts are half his.
He said half. Into a microphone. Ezra Kim, who once corrected a professor's footnote.
What does Brody do with the room's attention?
Name what Ezra built—just as specifically.
And the rent line exists because Ezra stayed up till three finding a lease we could afford. Somebody write that down.
My ears go hot. I push my glasses up with the wrong finger. The room laughs, kindly.
At the showcase, Brody and Ezra each publicly credited the other's specific work.
Thank him briefly. Ask to talk after.
Thanks, partner.
Offstage I catch his sleeve. “That was big. I want to say something back, just not into a mic. After?”
After. I'll be the one pretending I'm not waiting.
Brody thanked Ezra briefly on stage and asked to talk privately afterward.
Tell Coach no—on the record.
Afterward, Coach says he should've done the Iowa drive.
I did the Iowa drive, Coach. I'm doing what comes after. You should take a flyer.
You just told a football coach no. In public. I need to sit down.
Brody refused the coach's field-story script and told him so directly after the showcase.
Empty Bleachers
Ask him out—with no project as the excuse
The stadium, west bleachers, row 30
Wednesday, 9:10 PM
The stadium is dark for the off-season. Two jackets lie on the bleachers: a letterman and a hoodie from a lab Ezra hates.
I've practiced this. Out loud. In my truck. The truck thinks it went great.
Senior formal's Saturday. Come with me. No presentation. Just a terrible playlist.
I'm grading the playlist.
You're not grading me.
I stop. He means it exactly the way it sounds. He always does. It's the most unnerving thing about him.
I haven't graded you since October. I asked off your roster. I wrote “conflict of interest” and didn't elaborate.
October. That's before the drop form. That's before everything.
What does Brody do now?
Ask again, plainly. Wait for the answer.
So that's a conflict of interest. Is it a yes?
It's a yes. It's a yes with notes on the playlist.
Brody laughs so loud a motion light clicks on in the press box.
Brody asked Ezra to the senior formal as a date, and Ezra said yes.
Go as friends—for now. Say so.
Okay. Then come Saturday as my friend. I want whatever this is to go at the speed of real.
Friends. Correct speed. I'm still grading the playlist.
Brody invited Ezra to the formal as friends, choosing to take things slow.
Take it back. Give him room.
That's a lot to hear. I think I asked too fast. Forget Saturday. Not you. Saturday.
I nod. I pick up my hoodie. I leave his jacket folded where it was, which is its own kind of answer.
Brody withdrew the formal invitation to give them both room after Ezra's confession.
No Rubric
Make sure this invitation has no grade attached
Lou's Diner, the corner booth
Sunday, 8:05 AM
The morning after the formal, however it went, they've both ended up at Lou's. Brody's laptop stays zipped in his bag.
No slides?
No rubric.
I don't know how to be impressive here.
You could pass the syrup.
An achievable objective.
I pass it. Our fingers overlap on the handle one second longer than syrup requires.
And ask if I want to do this again.
What does Brody answer?
Say yes. Then ask him something, too.
Do you want to do this again? Pancakes, no agenda, next Sunday and possibly several after?
Yes. And I want to hold your hand on the walk back. Can I?
I say yes by holding out my hand. It's sticky. He takes it anyway.
Brody and Ezra both clearly agreed to keep seeing each other and held hands on the walk back.
Ask to go slower—or stay friends.
Yes to breakfast. I'm not sure about the rest yet. Can we keep it breakfast for a while?
Breakfast is a valid unit. I can work in breakfast.
Brody asked to keep things slow, breakfast only for now, and Ezra agreed.
Say no. Say goodbye kindly.
I don't think I want to do this again. I want to finish this term without wondering what you think of me.
I nod. It lands, and I let it. I pay my half and tip well, because he'd notice.
For the record, I thought a lot of you. Past tense is grammar, not feelings.
Brody declined to continue a private relationship, and they said a kind goodbye at the diner.

Decide what you are to each other after graduation
Venture Lab, the submission terminal
Friday of finals week, 11:48 PM

If I take it, I score your project. I won't grade you and then hold your hand at graduation. I won't.
Then don't. Or do, and we wait. What do you want?
Nobody asks me that. I usually just announce it.
Twelve minutes. You ask me first, I'll ask you second.
The cursor blinks in the signature field. Two names fit. So does one.
What does Brody choose?
Sign it together. Then ask him to dance.
I decline the judging seat. I type both names on the cover, in the order we did the work. His first.

We can be bad at this together.

Submit your own parts. Talk after graduation.

Independent Submission
Brody ends the team before either of them can decide for the other again. Two submissions go in at 11:59, and both of them graduate knowing exactly whose work is whose.
